articles.heading: The European Union’s approach toward trustworthy and safe AI | Communications Today
articles.content: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become deeply woven into the fabric of our daily lives, often in ways we may not even notice. From virtual assistants reminding us to take medication or playing our favorite genre of music, to AI-driven medical devices, telecom networks, and industrial processes automated through intelligent systems, AI is everywhere. The evolution of AI has progressed rapidly, delivering increasing benefits across various sectors as it continues to expand globally.In recent years, the adoption of AI has grown manifold across a wide range of sectors. This surge is driven mainly by advances in algorithms, computing techniques, the vast amounts of data generated through ICT—the digitization of systems—and the increasing affordability of high-performance processing power. These factors have collectively driven significant breakthroughs in AI technologies, including the development of large language models (LLMs) that have the potential to impact society profoundly.The European Union (EU) has taken a leading role globally toward shaping a comprehensive, ethical, and human-centric policy framework for AI. The EU approach is grounded in the belief that AI must serve people, not endanger their safety, respect fundamental rights, and align with European values of human rights, democracy, and the rule of law. The EU strategy supports a rules-based global order that strikes an adequate balance between innovation and public trust and safety.The High-Level Expert Group laid the EU’s ethical foundation for AI on AI (AI HLEG), which published Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI in 2019. In 2024, the EU formally adopted the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) — the world’s first comprehensive legal framework for AI, with full enforcement scheduled for 2026.The proposal for the new AI Regulation is set as a New-Legislative Framework (NLF) type legislation, which means the role of harmonized standards will be key, enabling economic operators to achieve compliance and ensure that AI systems are safe and trustworthy.As part of the European Commission’s Digital Strategy for shaping Europe’s digital future, the EU AI Office established its AI Board (an advisory forum providing technical expertise to the Board), which is playing a crucial role in the governance framework set out by the AI Act and ensuring the effective implementation of the AI Act across the European Union.Recently, the European Commission has also published advisory guidelines to assist providers of general-purpose AI models in meeting the requirements of the AI Act. The guidelines clarify obligations, providing legal certainty for all actors across the AI value chain, and complement the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice.The three European Standardisation Organisations (ESOs) — CEN, CENELEC, and ETSI — support and fully align with EU’s AI vision and its implementation. These standardisation bodies are working toward shaping a secure, responsible, and innovative AI future — one that safeguards users, advances technology, and nurtures trust in AI-powered telecommunications and beyond.CEN and CENELEC’s Joint Technical Committee 21 (JTC 21)  plays a central role in Europe in developing harmonized AI standards, supporting the EU AI Act requirements, particularly for high-risk AI systems. This is done via a mandate (M/613) given by the European Commission to CEN and CENELEC. These harmonised standards under development would provide a comprehensive framework covering AI Trustworthiness Framework, Risk Management, Quality Management, and AI Conformity assessment, apart from standards on datasets, bias, cybersecurity, and Natural Language Processing (Full work program).  CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 gathers over 300 experts from more than 20 countries working through five specialised groups: the Strategic Advisory Group (SAG), Operational, Engineering, Foundational and Societal Aspects, and Cybersecurity for AI Systems. Through a long-standing agreement between CEN/ISO and CENELEC/IEC, CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 can adopt or offer deliverables from or to ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 (an international subcommittee responsible for Artificial Intelligence). This ensures that European AI standardisation efforts are aligned with global standards while also addressing the region-specific requirements of the EU AI Act.ETSI is also at the forefront of shaping AI’s role in the digital arena. With its Technical Committee (TC) on Securing Artificial Intelligence (TC SAI), ETSI is elevating AI security through high-quality technical standards. This Committee of Experts is addressing four core aspects of Securing AI as a System Component, Mitigating AI-enabled threats, Leveraging AI to bolster security defences, always considering societal security and safety implications in AI’s deployment. One of its latest technical specifications includes ETSI TS 104 223 – Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI): Baseline Cybersecurity Requirements for AI Models and Systems. This standard sets a robust cybersecurity benchmark amid escalating cyber threats targeting AI systems. ETSI has also developed specifications to help operators facilitate their network deployment by utilizing AI techniques through its Industry Specification Group (ISG), under the label of Experiential Networked Intelligence (ENI). But AI systems need to be tested, and this is the role of  ETSI’s TC on Methods for Testing and Specification (TC MTS) , which focuses on the challenges of testing AI/ML systems. It has notably published a technical report on Test Methodology and Test Specification for AI-enabled Systems. Ongoing work targets specifications for Continuous Auditing-Based Conformity Assessment for AI-enabled systems, as well as a harmonised documentation scheme for trustworthy AI.Lastly, as part of its involvement in 3GPP together with India’s TSDSI and other regional partners, ETSI contributes to the development of 6G, the next generation of mobile communication systems in which AI is a foundational comp

articles.heading: Neuro-telecom  Brains over bits — Powering human-centric networks | Communications Today
articles.content: As an incumbent participant in the Indian telecom journey since beginning of the mobile generations, I have often wondered what the harbinger of next generational shift will be. As we stand at the beginning of yet another calendar year, let me create a mix of crystal ball gaze and my own wish list regarding the most exciting and fundamental shift, that to Neuro-telecommunications.Neuro telecommunication adds a powerful new layer: the ability to sense and respond to brain and physiological signals. Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs), neuromorphic AI at the edge, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) can allow networks to shape themselves around the user’s mental workload, emotional state, or medical needs—opening new frontiers in digital health, learning, and immersive communication. In this exciting phase, telecom networks are no longer just highways for bits; they are becoming extensions of the human brain, senses, and hence society.Traditional networks were engineered around cells, towers, and devices; success meant more Mbps and wider coverage. Human-centric networks invert this logic by treating people—their intent, cognition, and context—as the primary design anchors, with infrastructure adapting around them. In practical terms, this means optimizing not only for speed and latency, but for experience, accessibility, safety, and inclusion.While 5G laid the groundwork for the Internet of Things (IoT) and enterprise applications, 6G is being designed for the Internet of Senses. The primary technical barrier to Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) has always been latency. Human neurological processes occur at sub-millisecond speeds; any delay in data transmission doesn’t just cause “lag”—it causes physical disorientation. With 6G’s promise of sub-millisecond latency and terahertz-frequency bands, we are finally approaching “synaptic parity.” For the first time, the network will be fast enough to keep pace with human thought, allowing for the seamless transmission of neural signals over vast distances.From connectivity to human-centricityNeuro communication, integrates brain-inspired technologies like brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), neuromorphic computing, and neural networks into telecom systems, enabling human-centric networks that adapt to brain signals, cognitive states, and physiological data, aligned with 6G advancements. In India government-backed research is emphasizing affordable, sustainable connectivity fused with AI and neurotech for healthcare, rural access, and smart infrastructure.The transition to 6G represents more than a generational upgrade—it is a philosophical pivot. We are moving from Information Transfer (the movement of bits) to Knowledge Synthesis (the movement of intent). By merging Semantic Communication, Integrated Sensing (ISAC), and sub-millisecond neural parity, 6G is evolving into a proactiveGlobal Nervous System. This architecture doesn’t just connect devices; it closes the gap between human intent and digital execution, providing the first truly “empathetic” infrastructure in history.Neuro-telecommunications is the direct interfacing of Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) with cellular networks—which is the most complex R&D challenge till date. It requires a fundamental shift from bit-error-rate (BER) optimization to Neural-Latency-Parity.Global R&D is currently being undertaken in following technical streams:The Physical Layer (PHY) evolution— Sub-THz and latency.Current research led by the Hexa-X-II project (Europe) and the Next G Alliance (USA) is focused on the “Synaptic Gap” in network timing.The 1ms barrier.Human sensory-motor loops operate at ~10ms, but neural feedback for fine motor control requires <1ms air-interface latency.Waveform engineering.R&D is shifting toward Orthogonal Time Frequency Space (OTFS) waveforms, which are more resilient to the high-mobility and high-frequency doppler shifts found in the Terahertz (THz) bands (100 GHz – 3 THz) necessary for high-density neural dataNeural decoding at the edge.Semantic Intelligence Institutions like Stanford’s Neural Prosthetics Systems Lab and Kernel are moving toward “Semantic Neural Decoding.” Instead of transmitting raw EEG/ECoG signals, the network’s AI-Native Core uses Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) to decode motor intent locally at the Edge. This reduces the data backhaul requirements from several Gigabits of raw neural noise to a few kilobits ofIntent Vectors.The AI engine — Decoding the mindNeuro-telecommunications is not merely about “patching” a brain into a network. The human brain does not output clean digital packets; it produces a chaotic storm of electrical signals. This is where Generative AI becomes the critical translator.Integrated AI at the network edge will function as aNeural Interpreter. It will use sophisticated machine learning models to filter noise from intent, decoding raw brain activity into actionable data. Whether it isthinkinga text message orvisualizinga remote drone’s flight path, AI provides the semantic layer that makes neuro-connectivity intelligible to the digital world.Universal design — The ultimate tool for accessibilityThe most profound impact of this technology lies in significantly improving Accessibility for People with Disability. For the millions living with motor impairments, ALS, or spinal cord injuries, Neuro-telecommunications represents the ultimateequalizer. In fact, a watershed moment where the convergence of AI-native cores and sub-millisecond latency dismantles the traditional barriers between biological intent and digital execution thus bringing back dignity and self-control.Synthetic speech and mobility.Through 6G-enabled BCI, an individual who has lost the ability to speak can have their inner voice synthesized into real-time audio via the network. Similarly, the intent to move can be transmitted to smart exoskeletons or home automation systems instantaneously.Cognitive augmentation.AI can act as a cognitive prosthetic, helping those

articles.heading: Future of AI in network management — Transforming connectivity and efficiency | Communications Today
articles.content: Optimizing connectivity with AIThe telecom sector is facing margin pressures and rising costs, exacerbated by inflationary trends. To mitigate these challenges, telcos are increasingly turning to AI-powered solutions. AI enhances connectivity by optimizing network traffic, reducing latency, and improving reliability. Machine learning algorithms analyze vast amounts of data to predict and prevent network congestion, ensuring smooth and uninterrupted service for users.The integration of AI within network operations is not only transforming connectivity but also reshaping the telecom industry’s landscape. The surge in tech and digital investments reflects a strategic shift towards leveraging AI for competitive advantage. Telcos that embrace AI-driven solutions are better equipped to navigate the challenges posed by economic uncertainties and tariff increases.Impact of AI and Gen AI in Telecoms network performanceBy leveraging AI, the telecom industry is set to unlock new levels of efficiency and innovation, paving the way for a more connected and secure future.Optimized network managementAI’s real-time processing of large datasets enables telecom providers to manage their networks more efficiently. Predictive analytics are crucial in identifying potential issues before they escalate, allowing for proactive maintenance and reducing downtime. AI-driven network management systems can automate routine tasks, such as traffic routing and bandwidth allocation, leading to cost savings and improved service quality. Ericsson highlights that optimized networks enhance ROI, increasing user throughput by 15 percent during peak hours and cutting unplanned expansions by 10%.1Jio Platforms launched Jio Brain, integrating machine learning capabilities into telecom and enterprise networks. It provides over 500 APIs for ML-enabled services and advanced AI features across various media types, aiming to innovate 5G services, accelerate 6G development, and ensure future-proof efficiency gains.2Cost reduction and efficiencyInflationary pressures have forced telecom companies to explore innovative ways to reduce costs and maintain profitability. AI offers a viable solution by streamlining operations and enhancing resource utilization. Automated systems reduce the need for manual intervention, resulting in significant cost savings. Furthermore, AI’s predictive capabilities minimize downtime, ensuring consistent service delivery and customer satisfaction.Security and fraud detectionNetwork security is a paramount concern for telecom companies.Telecom fraudremains a pressing global concern, as highlighted by Communications Fraud Control Association (CFCA), which reported a 15% increase in fraud losses in 2024 compared to 2021, totalling an estimated US$38.9 billion lost, equivalent to 2.5% of telecom revenues3. AI algorithms play a crucial role in combating fraud, including SIM-swapping, unauthorized network access, fake profiles, and billing fraud. Machine learning models can detect unusual patterns in network traffic, flagging potential security breaches and fraudulent activities. By continuously learning from new data, AI systems become more adept at distinguishing between legitimate and malicious activities, thereby safeguarding sensitive information and infrastructure. For example, AI detects SIM-swapping by analysing patterns in SIM card usage.Airtel IQ and AT&T leverage AI and machine learning to bolster fraud prevention. Airtel IQ’s SpamShield, an AI/ML platform, detects and halts fraudulent messages for banks and fintech firms, ensuring secure interactions and protecting customer trust.4AT&T uses AI to analyse billions of daily calls, identifying patterns suggestive of robocalls. Suspected robocallers are flagged for human review to prevent blocking legitimate automated calls.5Dark NOC — The future of fully automated network operationsThe concept of Dark NOC (Network Operations Center) is gaining traction. A Dark NOC leverages Gen AI and machine learning to operate autonomously, minimizing the need for human intervention. By utilizing AI for automated monitoring, predictive maintenance, and security measures, Dark NOCs ensure optimal network functionality and resilience. According to TMForum’s estimates, GenAI driven end-to-end automated network operations can deliver the following improvements in operational metrics:More than 80% improvement in MTTD (Mean time to detect)More than 50% improvement in MTTR (Mean time to respond)More than 50% reduction in trouble ticketing80% reduction in customer complaintsAI in action– globally telcos are increasingly imbedding Dark NOC strategies in their overall network strategy to stay competitive and maintain high service standards.TelefonicaTelefonica, a telecom provider in Europe and Latin America, has been at the forefront of integrating AI to enhance its network operations. Telefónica’s Tech Digital Operations Center (DOC), monitors and operates its customers’ cybersecurity and cloud services globally, 24 hours a day, every day of the year. By leveraging AI, Telefonica has improved its predictive maintenance capabilities, reducing network downtime significantly. Additionally, AI has enabled Telefonica to optimize its resource allocation, leading to cost savings and increased operational efficiencyDeutsche Telekom (DT)Deutsche Telekom (DT) has invested heavily in AI to transform its network management processes. The company utilizes AI-driven analytics to monitor network performance in real-time and quickly respond to any anomalies. This proactive approach has resulted in enhanced service quality and customer satisfaction. DT’s AI initiatives have also focused on improving network security. By employing machine learning models, DT can detect and mitigate cyber threats more effectively, protecting its infrastructure and customer data. articles.heading: Agentic AI in Indian telecom — A deep-dive analysis | Communications Today
articles.content: India’s telecom sector is uniquely positioned to lead in large-scale adoption of agentic AI, driven by its unparalleled scale and rapid technological evolution. With over 1.1 billion wireless connections, India’s networks operate in one of the world’s most complex and demanding environments, where efficiency, agility, and personalization are critical. The aggressive roll-out of 5G, supported by nearly 500,000 base stations, is further accelerating the need for real-time, adaptive, and autonomous network management powered by AI.At the same time, intense business pressures—ranging from cost rationalization and competitive pricing to hyper-personalized customer experience and rapid digital inclusion—are pushing Indian telcos to explore next-generation AI solutions. Adding to this momentum is the explosive growth of data, fuelled by widespread smartphone penetration, affordable data plans, and the consumption of digital services, creating rich, diverse datasets ideal for AI-driven insights and automation.Nearly 50 percent of Indian telcos are deploying AI agents, while the rest are piloting multi-agent workflows spanning predictive maintenance, customer engagement, and network optimization. Notably, most operators have reported positive RoI from generative AI investments, especially in operations, fraud detection, and customer service automation. In particular, the Technology, Media, and Telecom (TMT) sector is leading this shift, utilizing AI to enhance operational efficiency, accelerate revenue growth, and deliver hyper-personalized customer experiences at scale.Strategic telco initiativesUse casesAgentic AI in telecom enables predictive maintenance and service assurance by monitoring hardware health—such as base stations, routers, and batteries—predicting failure trends, and automating preventive actions. This has resulted in reduced downtime, fewer service disruptions, and extended equipment lifecycles.Through hyper-personalized customer engagement, intelligent agents is able to unify data from calls, digital interactions, payment history, and social media to tailor customer experiences and proactively resolve issues. Applications include personalized plan recommendations, proactive recharge alerts, contextual offers, and regional language support.In fraud and threat detection, AI agents continuously analyze network traffic, SIM provisioning, billing systems, digital payments, and KYC processes for anomalies. These adaptive agents quickly respond to emerging fraud patterns, enabling rapid and multi-layered risk mitigation.Regulatory compliance and process automation are enhanced as agents manage cross-domain workflows such as regulatory reporting, settlements, and dispute resolution in real time with improved accuracy.The business value of Agentic AI is evident: operating expenses (OPEX) are reduced by close to 30 percent through field-force optimization and workflow automation. Service disruptions have showed decline by nearly 50 percent due to faster and smarter network issue resolution. Revenue growth is achieved through improved customer retention and accelerated rollout of new products and channels. Energy efficiency improvement with a 25–30 percent reduction in data center power consumption enabled by predictive operations. Customer satisfaction increased as average handling times decrease, resulting in a nearly 30 percent boost in Net Promoter Scores (NPS). Furthermore, fraud pre-emption significantly reduced SIM swap fraud and financial losses with real-time anomaly detection and alerts.Reliance JioThe JioBrain digital twin system runs constant simulations for capacity planning and provides early warnings of potential failures. The AI Cloud supports cross-industry agentic applications, such as smart grids, IoT security, and healthcare, while also enabling the reliable scaling of 5G with the lowest drop-off rates in both rural and urban circles, as well as offering dynamic, demand-sensitive pricing.AirtelBharti Airtel has implemented AI-driven spam call detection, which has resulted in a 49 percent reduction in subscriber complaints to date.  In collaboration with Nokia, Airtel has deployed agentic AI for unified 4G/5G network management and zero-touch maintenance. Additionally, Nxtra data centers feature AI-driven thermal and power management, contributing to Airtel’s sustainability targets.Vodafone IdeaVodafone Idea has adopted HCL’s ANA platform for agentic automation, enabling self-healing networks, seamless VoLTE, and flexible resource allocation. The company has strategically pivoted to agentic systems as it secures spectrum for its delayed 5G rollout.TelcoPlatform/InitiativeImpactJioJioBrain, AI CloudDigital twin for network simulation, predictive maintenance, real-time optimization. AI Cloud democratizes access across India’s enterprisesAirtelNxtra, Nokia PartnershipAgentic AI drives energy-efficient data centers, AI-powered spam detection, and network self-optimization. Collaboration with Nokia for advanced 5G AI infrastructureVodafone IdeaHCL’s ANA PlatformAgentic workflow automation for VoLTE, network ops, service reliability, and CX improvementsAgentic AI – Architecture, challenges and regulationsArchitecture.Agentic AI operates through four layers—Perception (multi-modal data fusion from sensors, logs, and digital sources), Reasoning (knowledge graphs, rule engines, and graph neural networks for contextual inference), Planning (dynamic policy planners allocating resources based on priorities), and Execution (automated systems pushing real-time changes to OSS/BSS and CX platforms).Challenges.Key hurdles include data silos and legacy integration, scalability across Bharat-scale networks, and latency requirements for autonomous 5G and IoT.Security and ethics.Risks involve AI model bias, cybersecurity threats, and privacy concerns in managing personal data across complex ecosystems.Policy support.TRAI and DoT drive AI adoption via compliance frameworks, Right of Way rule

articles.heading: Six AI predictions for 2026 | Communications Today
articles.content: More code and more access to AI tools will make the tech look very different next year.Every company should be preparing for the landscape shifts that AI will bring in 2026. AI has already transformed entire industries, and its rate of acceleration is paving the way for even more advancement in 2026.We work with AI every day and have to stay ahead of the progressions to stay competitive. We see trends, help companies (including ourselves) unlock its value, and build tech that’s driving the next wave of AI innovation.Here’s what I think 2026 is going to hold for AI, increasing its impact on technology, businesses and society. These predictions are largely driven by two technologies combined: AI agents and AI-fueled coding. The power of these technologies together is democratizing AI, putting world class AI power into even more hands!Fine-tuned SLMs will become the most-used models by enterprises.Fine-tuned small language models are built for specific purposes and trained on focused data, providing high accuracy for their specialized tasks. They’re breaking the old adage: “Between good, cheap and fast, choose two.” These SLMs can provide all three benefits compared to their large language counterparts, often performing very comparatively with the larger, more generalized models in terms of accuracy and outperforming with speed and costs.It’s why businesses are increasingly relying on them. The large language and reasoning models will often handle the master control of an agentic workflow, but the purpose-built SLMs very adequately deliver the required accuracy and efficiency when trained for their dedicated job within the agentic workflow.Across the board, businesses will understand the importance of their own data in driving AI value. Fine-tuned SLMs are key to unlocking that value in mature agentic solutions.AI-fueled coding will be the next major development methodology, reducing some development cycles to just minutes.AI tools have been helping developers for years, handling repetitive tasks, generating boilerplate code and debugging programs. AI-fueled coding will be the next big methodology, bringing the spirit of agile coding into its next evolution. This will tangibly redefine the software development cycle, shortening development timelines, increasing production-grade output and enabling teams to focus on higher-level problem solving.With AI-fueled coding, developers will start to wear multiple hats in the lifecycle, from product owners to architects, reducing cycle times and time to operation. As AI gets better, the best cases will see products or apps built in basically one shot, with very few human edits.We’ve used AI-fuel coding ourselves to build an internal curated data product in 20 minutes, when it would have taken 6 weeks without AI. And importantly, our AI-fueled coding framework is trained to adhere to our rigorous code discipline for quality, security, and compliance.Non-technical teams can get in on the development process now too, using plain language prompts to build software prototypes. Then AI-fueled coding can turn it into a full product, with true production grade code, within hours instead of weeks.Businesses will begin building on-demand apps, supported by AI agents.Most business applications have traditionally required long development cycles, continued investment, and constant maintenance. AI-fueled coding dramatically accelerates software development cycles, making it feasible for a company to build on-demand apps!Autonomous agents can even independently adapt to new requirements, making redevelopment faster than traditional app cycles. Businesses can respond faster to changing needs, experiment with new solutions, and pivot away from legacy apps that require long-term investment.Traditional apps won’t completely disappear…yet. The ability to launch and iterate on-demand functionality, in a fraction of the time, leveraging agentic AI will enable a more agile and cost-effective choice for immediate business challenges than traditional models in many situations.Private high capacity, low latency fiber networks will connect enterprises to consolidated compute centers.Computing relies on connectivity.  With AI, complex computing needs to be faster than ever before. Companies are re-evaluating their cloud strategies to make the most out of AI, but they will also be looking at their connectivity.We’ll see an increase in private high-speed fiber networks built for major enterprises who are investing in AI. This will connect businesses to their cloud and compute centers with the fastest connectivity speeds and dedicated pathways.When they have these pathways, we’ll also see cloud companies consolidate their cloud centers close to where private networks exist. Cloud centers could likely move closer to the premises, in a new era of cloud, hybrid-cloud and on-prem networking.Telcos will offer more AI services, like fine-tuning, to business customers.There are few industries that deal with data on the scale of telecommunication companies. We’re well-versed in training large and small models, and we work with major cloud and AI software providers, giving us a strong foundation in AI services like fine-tuning.To be clear, we’re not announcing anything available from AT&T. But we have mastered fine-tuning models on our network data, and have a long history in how we manage, process and secure massive datasets. I believe the foundation and the market demand is there to extend telco services out of core connectivity and cloud hosting, into productized AI services.By helping business customers tailor their AI needs, telecom companies can open up new revenue streams and expand their already essential role in the AI-powered business landscape.Metrics for AI accuracy, cost and speed will become the focus across every business sector.With the democratization of development tools comes the spread of AI business metrics. AI is shifting from a novelty into a necessity in every indu

articles.heading: 5 biggest Gen AI stories of 2025 in India | Communications Today
articles.content: India didn’t have a “ChatGPT moment” in 2025. It had a scale moment. This was the year GenAI stopped being a demo culture story and became a language, distribution, and infrastructure story.These are the five that actually moved the needle in India in 2025.1. Local-language AI became the real frontier, not English benchmarksLanguage as infrastructureIndia’s GenAI race wasn’t about English chatbots. It was about Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Marathi, Kannada, and voice-first use cases.Government-backed programs like BHASHINI pushed AI access across 22 scheduled languages, while private players trained and fine-tuned Indic-focused models designed for code-mixed speech and regional syntax. Models supporting 8–12 Indian languages became table stakes, not differentiators.This wasn’t ideology. It was math. Recent industry reporting shows 98 percent of users access Indic-language content, and ~57 percent of urban users prefer consuming content in regional languages, and most first-time AI users interact through voice or mobile keyboards, not clean text prompts. Many Indic-focused models and platforms emphasized coverage across multiple Indian languages (often 8–12+), shifting the conversation from ‘can it speak Hindi?’ to ‘does it work reliably across dialects?Sovereign AI became realA quieter but structurally important shift in 2025 was India’s move from talking about AI sovereignty to actually building it. Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government positioned BharatGen as a publicly funded, homegrown multimodal foundation model, launched on June 2, 2025, designed to support 22 Indian languages across text, speech, and translation use cases. A month earlier, on April 26, 2025, the government selected Sarvam to build India’s sovereign large language model, marking a clear decision to develop core model capability domestically rather than rely entirely on foreign frontier providers. Together, these moves signaled that for India, language access was no longer just an application-layer problem—it had become a strategic infrastructure priority, tied to data sovereignty, cost control, and long-term AI independence.We learned that in India, accuracy across dialects is product-market fit. Miss the language, you miss the market.2. IndiaAI stopped being policy and started behaving like infrastructure2025 was the year India treated AI like national infrastructure, not just an innovation theater.Compute moved from promise to procurementThe IndiaAI Mission moved into execution with an approved outlay of roughly ₹10,300–10,400 crore (~$1.2B), explicitly targeting domestic compute capacity, startup access, and public-private GPU infrastructure. Early plans referenced 10,000+ GPUs, with later government commentary signaling ambitions far beyond that. Round-2 tender bids offered ~18,000 GPUs (expected ~15,000 accepted after evaluation).This matters because India doesn’t lack talent. It lacks cheap, available, local compute.Why it mattered: When GPUs become accessible, you unlock fine-tuning, inference at scale, and enterprise pilots that don’t die in procurement.Regulation clarified deployment boundariesWhat also shifted in 2025 was regulatory clarity. With the notification of India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules, AI deployment stopped living in a legal gray zone. The rules formalized consent, data minimization, breach reporting, and accountability requirements that directly shape how GenAI systems can be trained, deployed, and audited inside India. For enterprises, this didn’t slow adoption—it narrowed it.Use cases moved away from open-ended experimentation and toward governed workflows, enterprise copilots, and internal automation where data lineage and access controls could be enforced. In practice, regulation didn’t block GenAI in India; it defined where it could safely operate, accelerating serious deployments while quietly killing irresponsible ones.3. Indian GenAI startups matured, and funding followed execution, not hypeIndia’s GenAI startup ecosystem grew up fast in 2025. By mid-year, cumulative funding in Indian GenAI startups reached ~$1B, with roughly 30 percent year-over-year growth. But the signal wasn’t just the money. It waswhereit went.The startups that raised weren’t selling “AI assistants.” They were selling workflow software, vertical AI, and systems that worked at Indian price points.At the high end, India also proved it could price AI-native ambition aggressively. Finally, the lesson of 2025: India stopped copying Silicon Valley demos and started shipping operational AI.4. Telecom showed what GenAI looks like at population scaleIf you want to understand how AI actually reached people in India in 2025, don’t look at apps, look at the telecom network.The clearest example is Bharti Airtel’s AI-powered spam detection, which rolled out at the network level, not as a consumer product. This system analyzes calling and messaging patterns in real time at a massive scale and automatically flags suspicious calls and texts. Airtel disclosed that it processes around one trillion records, identifies tens of millions of spam calls per day, and expanded alerts into multiple Indian languages so warnings are understandable, not just visible. The reception wasn’t excitement. It was relief. Fewer interruptions. Fewer scams. No settings to configure. AI didn’t ask for attention—it quietly did its job.Vodafone Idea followed a similar path, deploying AI-based spam SMS detection across its network. Vi reported flagging hundreds of millions of spam messages, using AI to identify abnormal traffic patterns rather than relying on user complaints. For an operator under financial pressure, this wasn’t innovation theater. It was basic hygiene—using AI like a pressure valve to keep the system from breaking. Customers didn’t praise the AI. They just noticed fewer junk messages clogging their phones.Across the industry, Indian telecom treated AI the way plumbing is treated in a city: invisible when it wor

articles.heading: The art of recovery — Forging unbreakable resilience in the face of cyber threats | Communications Today
articles.content: In today’s hyperconnected and AI-accelerated digital economy, the question is no longer if an enterprise will face a cyberattack – but when, how severe, and how fast it can recover. Traditional cybersecurity approaches that emphasized perimeter defense, patching, and incident response are now insufficient in the face of advanced persistent threats, zero-day exploits, and AI-enabled attack vectors. The new frontier is cyber resilience – a proactive, recovery-centric approach that combines readiness, adaptability, and intelligent remediation. It is no longer enough to block threats; organizations must master the art of recovery.Redefining resilience in the cyber era.Cyber resilience is not just about having a good firewall or the latest endpoint protection tools. It is a holistic capability – one that blends technology, people, and processes to withstand disruptions, maintain operational continuity, and recover with precision. The rise of ransomware-as-a-service, deepfake-based social engineering, and AI-powered malware has escalated both the frequency and sophistication of attacks. Organizations must now operate under the assumption of compromise and shift their security postures from prevent-only to prepare-and-recover.Recovery, in this context, is not a one-time restoration event. It’s an ongoing discipline – rooted in business continuity planning, automated incident response, and adaptive threat intelligence. It requires organizations to maintain real-time situational awareness, quantify the blast radius of an attack, and enable systems to revert to known-good states with minimal disruption.The AI dimension — Double-edged sword.Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays a paradoxical role in the cybersecurity ecosystem. On one hand, threat actors are leveraging generative AI to scale phishing attacks, craft polymorphic malware, and identify system vulnerabilities with surgical precision. On the other hand, defenders are using AI to power predictive threat modeling, autonomous threat hunting, and automated incident response.Embedding AI into recovery strategies allows organizations to detect anomalies faster, prioritize threats by business impact, and accelerate forensic investigations. For example, AI-driven analytics can correlate logs from thousands of endpoints in real time to isolate an attack’s entry point. Machine learning models can simulate recovery paths and recommend the least disruptive remediation plan based on historical data and current context.More advanced use cases involve AI agents coordinating recovery activities autonomously – like restoring compromised services from clean backups, isolating affected systems from the network, and notifying compliance teams of potential breaches. AI thus becomes not just a guardian of enterprise systems but a partner in resilience engineering.Building blocks of recovery-driven cyber resilienceBusiness-aligned risk quantification.Cybersecurity spending must evolve from cost-center thinking to value-driven investments. Quantifying cyber risk in financial terms – such as potential revenue loss, downtime costs, or reputational damage – helps boards and CXOs justify strategic spending on recovery capabilities. Cyber resilience frameworks like FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) can help translate technical risk into business impact.Digital twin-based simulation for recovery readiness.Enterprises can now use digital twins – virtual replicas of systems and infrastructure – to simulate attack scenarios and test recovery strategies without impacting production environments. AI models can stress-test these simulations by injecting various threat vectors and observing system response, allowing organizations to fine-tune their playbooks.Cyber recovery vaults and immutable backups.Modern recovery strategies demand more than just routine backups. Organizations need cyber recovery vaults – isolated and air-gapped environments where critical data and configurations are stored in immutable formats. AI tools can monitor access patterns to these vaults and trigger alerts if anomalies are detected, ensuring that the last line of defense is not silently compromised.Human resilience and continuous learning.No recovery plan is complete without the human dimension. From SOC analysts and recovery engineers to non-technical staff, cyber resilience hinges on awareness, training, and collaboration. AI-based gamification tools and real-time simulated phishing platforms can improve cyber hygiene while ensuring that teams are battle-tested and recovery-ready.The strategic shift — From reactive to regenerative.Recovery must be reframed not as a damage control exercise but as a strategic enabler of trust and agility. A resilient organization can confidently pursue digital transformation, knowing it has the agility to recover from setbacks with minimal friction. Moreover, customers, partners, and regulators are increasingly expecting transparency and accountability in cyber preparedness. Those that embed recovery into their core digital fabric will not only reduce the impact of cyber incidents but also earn a reputational premium in the market.Just as physical infrastructure is built to withstand earthquakes and floods, digital infrastructure must now be built to recover – seamlessly, smartly, and securely. This requires a cultural shift, sustained investment, and deep integration of AI across the cybersecurity lifecycle.Recovery as a competitive advantage.In the age of intelligent threats and digital hyper-dependence, recovery is no longer a contingency – it is a core business capability. The art of recovery blends foresight, automation, and adaptability, enabled by AI and anchored in business priorities. Organizations that master this art will not only survive the next breach – they will emerge stronger, more trusted, and more competitive. In a world of escalating cyber threats, resilience is the new defense – and recovery is its sharpest tool. Redefining resilience

articles.heading: India faces 1 million AI talent shortfall by 2027 as demand outpaces supply | Communications Today
articles.content: India is staring at a structural shortage of AI talent, with demand from startups and enterprises far outpacing the pool of engineers capable of building and deploying production-grade systems. As generative AI, automation and AI-led solutions move from pilots to large-scale deployment, companies are finding that their growth plans are constrained not by capital or demand, but by the availability of experienced practitioners who can operate in regulated, high-stakes environments like BFSI and enterprise voice AI.​Recent analysis suggests the gap will widen sharply over the next few years: India could have more than 2.3 million AI job openings by 2027 but only around 1.2 million suitably qualified professionals, implying over one million roles may remain unfilled if current trends persist. Industry leaders note that the problem is most acute at the intersection of generative AI, natural language processing and systems engineering, where estimates indicate there may be roughly one capable GenAI engineer for every ten open positions, especially in applied AI and MLOps-heavy roles. This scarcity is magnified for startups, which struggle to match large firms on compensation and brand pull, even as they compete in the same narrow talent pool.​The crunch is not unique to India; globally, high-profile AI companies are seeing huge interest but making very selective hires, underscoring how thin the pipeline of deployment-ready AI specialists really is. At the same time, rapid salary inflation—particularly for GenAI and MLOps roles, where compensation has reportedly jumped by more than 50 percent in recent years—combined with candidates’ preference for narrowly defined or research-centric roles, is making it harder for emerging firms to fill positions that demand end-to-end ownership, governance and scale considerations.​In response, startups are shifting strategy from pure hiring to a mix of selective recruitment and aggressive capability building. Many are maintaining rolling hiring pipelines for critical AI roles, bringing people on board ahead of visible demand, while investing heavily in internal training, cross-skilling and reusable platforms that let small teams deliver leveraged impact instead of simply expanding headcount. Campus partnerships, hackathons and focused outreach are being used to identify high-potential talent earlier, and several founders emphasize tighter screening and in-house training to convert promising generalists into deployment-ready AI engineers.​Executives broadly expect hiring to remain challenging in the near term as three forces reinforce each other: limited supply of experienced AI engineers, escalating pay benchmarks and the need for adaptable, cross-functional talent who can work across models, infrastructure, reliability and compliance. With demand for AI solutions still rising, this one-million-person talent shortfall is emerging as a key bottleneck for India’s AI growth story, and it is pushing startups to treat talent development and retention as a core strategic function rather than a supporting HR activity.​CT Bureau Recent analysis suggests the gap will widen sharply over the next few years: India could have more than 2.3 million AI job openings by 2027 but only around 1.2 million suitably qualified professionals, implying over one million roles may remain unfilled if current trends persist. articles.heading: Anthropic's AI push raises analyst concerns over IT services revenues | Communications Today
articles.content: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, triggered in part by Anthropic’s latest automation push, could structurally erode the IT sector’s high-margin application services revenues, creating downside risks to earnings and valuations, analysts warn.Shares in India’s software exporters fell 0.7 per cent on Thursday, a day after plunging 6 per cent in their worst session for nearly six years, as AI-driven automation from US-based Anthropic and Palantir fuelled fears of compressed project timelines and disruption to the industry’s labour-intensive business model.The weakness has echoed across global IT stocks this week, extending a broader selloff in companies seen as most exposed to potential AI disruption.“There is more pain ahead for Indian IT,” Jefferies said, adding that Anthropic’s and Palantir’s claims highlight how AI could potentially erode application service revenues for IT firms.“With application services accounting for 40–70 per cent of revenues, firms face growth pressures, and consensus growth estimates do not fully reflect this, posing downside risks to valuations.”Indian IT firms have been ramping up AI investments and re-skilling efforts, even as weak global tech spending, delayed client decision-making and pricing pressure have weighed on the sector. Foreign investors offloaded a record $8.5 billion worth of Indian IT stocks in 2025.However, some analysts said the sharp selloff may be overdone.JPMorgan said that while concerns around AI disruption were not without merit, it was illogical to extrapolate the launch of some tools to an expectation that companies will replace every layer of mission-critical enterprise software.Domestic brokerage Kotak Institutional Equities described the decline as a case of “plenty of panic over a little flutter”.Among large IT firms, Tata Consultancy Services, Tech Mahindra and LTIMindtree have higher exposure to application services, which account for about 55 per cent–60 per cent of revenues, while HCL Tech has the lowest exposure at around 40 per cent.Their stocks fell between 4 per cent and 7 articles.heading: Modern telecommunications companies and major challenges facing chief executives | Communications Today
articles.content: In recent decades, the telecommunications industry has undergone significant transformation, progressing from providers of conventional voice services to key contributors in digital connectivity. The deployment of 5G networks, increasing complexity of data privacy regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and the proliferation of streaming platforms including Netflix and Spotify have markedly influenced operational models and customer engagement strategies within telecom companies. Present-day telecom organisations face a complex environment characterised by rapid technological innovation, evolving regulatory frameworks, and dynamic consumer preferences. In this context, Chief Experience Officers (CXOs) encounter substantial challenges, managing the coordination of seamless customer experiences amid technological change and regulatory developments. Their scope of responsibility encompasses not only customer service but also the integration of emerging technologies, ensuring regulatory compliance, and sustaining competitiveness in a persistently evolving sector.Technological disruption — Navigating innovation and costThe telecommunications sector is undergoing relentless technological disruption, exemplified by the global rollout of 5G networks and the proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT). A notable case is one of UK’s leading mobile operators’ strategic investment in 5G infrastructure across the UK and Europe, which has enabled the company to launch low-latency, high-speed services for both consumers and enterprise clients. However, these advancements come with considerable capital outlays and integration hurdles, particularly when harmonising new systems with legacy networks. Similarly, EU’s largest telcos’ deployment of AI-driven network management has improved operational efficiency but required significant upfront investment in both technology and workforce reskilling.To balance innovation with prudent cost management, executives can adopt frameworks such as the “Dual Transformation” model. This approach involves sustaining core business operations (Transformation A) while simultaneously investing in disruptive technologies and new business models (Transformation B). Leaders should prioritise pilot programmes and phased rollouts to validate technological investments before large-scale deployment, as demonstrated by a UK leading telco, incremental introduction of IoT-enabled smart city solutions in Manchester. Rigorous ROI analyses, strategic partnerships, and agile procurement processes are essential to controlling costs while keeping pace with rapid technological change. Executive decision-making should be grounded in data-driven scenario planning, enabling a proactive rather than reactive stance.Customer expectations and experience — balancing automation and human touchRising customer expectations are reshaping the competitive landscape. For instance, EE’s “My EE” app leverages advanced analytics to deliver personalised recommendations and real-time support, significantly improving customer satisfaction scores. Conversely, some operators have faced backlash from over-automating customer service channels, leading to frustration when users cannot reach a human agent for complex enquiries. The case of EU’s one of the largest telcos hybrid support models, which combine AI-powered chatbots with easy escalation to live representatives, illustrates a balanced approach that enhances efficiency without sacrificing personal connection.Executives can employ frameworks such as the “Customer Journey Mapping” methodology to identify critical touchpoints where human interaction is most valued, reserving automation for routine tasks. Investment in staff training to foster digital empathy and problem-solving skills ensures that personal interactions are meaningful and effective. Additionally, regular feedback loops—such as Net Promoter Score (NPS) tracking and real-time sentiment analysis—allow leadership to continuously refine the balance between automation and human service. By embedding these strategies into organisational culture, telecom leaders can meet evolving customer demands while maintaining operational excellence and cost-effectiveness.Regulatory complianceTelecom entities operate within a highly regulated environment, requiring CXOs to effectively manage a multifaceted landscape of policies, regulations, and compliance obligations at local, national, and international levels. With governments continually enacting new regulations related to data privacy, spectrum allocation, and market competition, telecom executives must ensure strict organizational compliance to mitigate the risk of significant financial penalties and reputational harm. Furthermore, adherence to compliance requirements may impede innovation, as companies often adopt a more cautious approach under increased regulatory scrutiny.Cybersecurity threats and strategic responsesWith the increasing interconnectivity made possible by services like IoT and 5G, telecom organizations are becoming more attractive targets for cyberattacks. CXOs must prioritize cybersecurity to protect sensitive customer data and ensure the integrity of their networks. Implementing robust security measures while maintaining user experience presents a considerable challenge. The balance between security and accessibility is paramount; organizations must invest in advanced security protocols and continually educate their workforce on best practices to thwart cyber threats.Talent acquisition and retentionThe telecom sector is grappling with a talent shortage in specialized fields such as network engineering, cybersecurity, and data analytics. CXOs need to create attractive workplace cultures to attract and retain top talent. This involves not only competitive compensation but also fostering an inclusive environment that encourages innovation and professional growth. Investing in training and development programs is esse

articles.heading: China accelerates energy expansion, seen as crucial to AI race | Communications Today
articles.content: New data on China’s relentless energy installations underscore warnings from Elon Musk and Jensen Huang that the nation’s world-beating power network will deliver a major advantage over the US in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.Since 2021, China has added more power capacity across all energy technologies than the US has in its history, including 543 gigawatts last year, according to figures released late last month by the country’s National Energy Administration.China will add more than 3.4 terawatts of electricity generation capacity over the next five years, almost six times as much as the US, BloombergNEF projects under its base-case Economic Transition Scenario. That influx would give the No. 2 economy greater ability to accommodate rising power demand from data centers.“The limiting factor for AI deployment is fundamentally electrical power,” Musk told BlackRock Inc. Chief Executive Officer Larry Fink in an interview at the World Economic Forum on Jan. 22. “Very soon, maybe even later this year we’ll be producing more chips than we can turn on — except for China,” said Tesla Inc. CEO Musk, whose xAI is building US data centers. “China’s growth in electricity is tremendous.”Musk’s comments echo similar sentiments from Nvidia Corp.’s CEO Huang, who has also identified access to electricity as a potential differentiator between the US and China. AI competitiveness can be thought of as a cake composed of five layers: energy, chips, infrastructure, models and applications, Huang told a December event hosted by the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “At the lowest level — energy — China has twice the amount of energy we have as a nation,” he said.In the US, data centers will account for 38% of the growth in electricity demand between 2024 and 2030, though just 6% in China, according to BNEF projections. Data centers will command almost 7% of total US power demand by 2030, compared to 2% in China.China, where electricity consumption hit a record last year, is continuing to rapidly add new power capacity with huge deployments of renewable sources like solar and wind alongside more coal, nuclear and gas facilities. Solar generating capacity is on track to surpass coal in China for the first time this year, though newly added renewables have lower utilization rates than fossil fuel assets.Growth in generation capacity is proving slower in the US, where electricity demand has recently begun surging after roughly two decades of flat growth through the early 2020s. The anticipated requirements from AI have triggered a rush of development of new gas-fired capacity, though US power plants can take years to come online as a result of more onerous regulation and supply chain bottlenecks. President Donald Trump’s opposition to renewables also means clean energy projects have been subject to cancellation or delays.“The federal government is essentially shooting ourselves in the foot by not allowing a more straightforward and robust uptake of” renewables to meet data center demand, said Michael Davidson, an associate professor at UC San Diego who focuses on US and Chinese energy policy.Already, snarls across the US power grid are becoming a drag on the AI industry. Some US utilities are telling data centers it will take years for them to connect, while northern Virginia — a major global hub for the sector — has experienced instances of disconnections as a result of grid faults. The mismatch of AI power demand and slower growth in capacity additions could trigger effective electricity shortfalls in some US markets by 2030, BNEF said in a December report.In contrast, connecting to the grid is “a non-issue in China” for new data centers, according to David Fishman, a Shanghai-based principal at consultancy The Lantau Group.China is likely to have spare power capacity equal to more than three times the world’s entire data center demand by 2030, according to Goldman Sachs Group Inc. analysts. A lack of similar capacity “could act as a bottleneck for further data center developments in the US,” analysts including Hongcen Wei wrote in the November note.Concerns about power availability mean it’s “extremely common” that energy is now the factor that is dictating AI developers’ growth in the US, said Samantha Gross, director of the energy security and climate initiative at the Brookings Institution.“The AI industry talks about time to power because that’s what’s rate-determining for them,” she said. “It’s not chip availability, it’s availability of power.”AI will account for a smaller share of total power demand in China than the US in part because of the impact of the Asian nation’s other energy-hungry sectors, including industry and electric vehicles — both of which will add electricity consumption at a faster rate through 2030.Still, energy access isn’t the only factor that’s likely to determine success in the AI sector, and the US retains its own advantages. articles.heading: The emerging trends in India's telecom sector — From 5G monetization to 6G aspirations | Communications Today
articles.content: Following one of the world’s fastest 5G rollouts, culminating in over 500,000 5G sites and 400 million users as of Sep-25, the Indian telecom sector is undergoing a structural shift. The narrative is moving decisively from capital-intensive network deployment to a multi-pronged strategy focused on monetization, operational efficiency, and future-looking R&D. Four key trends define this new phase: 1) The aggressive pursuit of the home broadband market via Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) and Unlicensed Band Radio (UBR); 2) A definitive pivot to high-margin enterprise solutions, validated by tangible private 5G and industrial IoT deployments; 3) The deep integration of AI and cloud-native architecture to reduce OpEx and build new “Techco” platforms; and 4) A clear, policy-driven national ambition to shape 6G and satellite communication standards.The new home broadband battleground: FWA and UBRWith 5G coverage established, the first major monetization vector is the fixed broadband market. Operators are using 5G FWA to bypass the high cost and slow pace of last-mile fiber deployment, directly targeting India’s ~190 million television-equipped homes (FICCI EY 2025).Reliance Jio:Jio has been aggressive in this segment. Its cloud-native 5G core, developed with AWS, is built to support FWA, UBR, and IoT services at scale (GSMA 5G Use Cases). This architecture already supports 9.5million 5G FWA subscribers. The company is also leveraging UBR, allowing it to scale home connectivity without straining its licensed spectrum holdings.Bharti Airtel:Airtel also sees FWA as a key strategic priority. Its “Airtel AirFiber” product is positioned to capture demand in non-metro regions where fiber penetration is low.According to TRAI data, FWA services (from all operators) contributed approximately 0.9 million of the 1.24 million new home broadband additions in September 2025. This wireless-led broadband expansion is significantly increasing the addressable market for operators, though it carries future capex risk related to network capacity and spectrum congestion if demand scales indiscriminately.The enterprise Pivot: Validated industrial use casesThe second, and potentially more lucrative, monetization front is the B2B enterprise segment. After years of theoretical use cases, operators are now deploying proven, high-performance solutions for industrial clients, as documented in the GSMA’s “5G in Action” report (Sep-25).Private 5G networks:This is the flagship enterprise offering, replacing traditional Wi-Fi in demanding environments.Manufacturing: Airtel deployed India’s first 5G-ready private network for a smart factory. The network delivers 99.9% uptime and 20-25 ms latency, supporting over 1,500 connected devices for automation and AI-based inspection—a level of reliability Wi-Fi could not provide.Mining:A private 5G network was deployed by Tidal Wave Technologies at Coal India sites in Ranchi and Dhanbad. The network enables critical safety and productivity applications, including drone-based surveying with 10 kg payloads and real-time IoT gas and environmental monitoring.Sector-specific 5G solutions:Manufacturing:Vi Business has partnered with L&T Heavy Engineering to deploy a private 5G network at the ‘A M Naik Heavy Engineering Complex’ in Hazira, Surat.Agriculture:Jio has deployed 5G-powered drones with multi-spectral cameras to scan fields. The images are shared in real-time over the 5G network, analyzed by AI/ML algorithms, and used for precision inputs.Healthcare:Airtel’s 5G Smart Clinics use a 5G and SD-WAN architecture to power cloud-based telemedicine platforms, enabling high-definition remote diagnostics in rural and underserved areas.These deployments confirm that 5G is solving specific industrial challenges related to latency, reliability, and device density, establishing a clear value proposition for enterprise clients.The “Telco-to-Techco” Shift: AI, cloud, and data centersThis trend details how operators are enabling new services while managing costs. The focus is on moving from connectivity providers to integrated technology companies (Techcos).AI for OpEx Control: Operators are using AI to optimize network efficiency.Airtel: Is targeting an estimated Rs1 billion in annual OpEx savings by using AI algorithms to put idle radios to sleep during low-traffic periods.Vodafone Idea:Its Value Engineering Centre has reportedly saved Rs0.49 billion in FY25 by using AI and analytics to revive and redeploy equipment that was previously written off.AI for revenue generation (Platforms):Jio:RIL recent AGM highlights the “JioBrain” platform, an in-house GenAI and digital-twin platform. This is built on the cloud-native 5G core which, per the GSMA report, is validated for AI/ML-driven automation and quantum-safe security, offered as a service to third parties.Airtel:The company is scaling its “Xtelify” platform, which evolved from an internal tool into a commercial AI suite for other telcos and enterprises. This is complemented by its Airtel IQ (CPaaS) business and leveraging its data engine to credit-score over 90 million users for financial services.Data center backbone: This AI and cloud transition is supported by massive investment in data centers.Airtel (Nxtra):Is planning a Rs 6,000 crore investment over the next four years and has partnered with Google to develop a gigawatt-scale data center campus in Visakhapatnam.Reliance:Announced its foray into the data center segment during its AGM, with plans for 3GW of AI-ready capacity, a significant-scale plan compared to the country’s current capacity. This data center will be powered by green energy.Adani:Through its joint venture company AdaniConneX, it announced a landmark partnership to develop a large AI data centre campus and new green energy infrastructure in Visakhapatnam.The policy & R&D horizon: 6G, satcom, and standardizationThe final trend is a forward-looking, policy-driven push to secure India’s position in the next generation of telecom. articles.heading: Telecom in the age of AI, cloud and sovereignty — Why India’s networks are becoming strategic national assets | Communications Today
articles.content: For over  three decades, India’s telecommunications sector was largely judged by coverage maps across the nation , call drops, and the price of a gigabyte. In 2026, that lens is outdated. Telecom networks are no longer just “dumb pipes” carrying everyone else’s innovation—they are becoming critical national infrastructure that determines how India  competes in AI, cloud, cybersecurity, digital public services, and even more importantly geopolitical resilience given the current geopolitical challenges that we are confronted with.India is a front-row case study and the scale is staggering. India’s 5G rollout has reached near-universal coverage, with services now available in 99.9 percent of the country’s districts as per the Govt of India data, and operators have installed over 5.18 lakh 5G base transceiver stations (BTS) as of Dec 31, 2025 as per DoT (Department of Telecommunications) year-end review report. At the same time, India has operationalised the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP) through the notification of the DPDP Rules, 2025, signalling a new era where data protection is not a corporate checkbox but an ecosystem-wide operating model.  And powering all of this is a “hard infra” surge: India’s operational data centre capacity is now 1.5 GW as of Dec 2025 as per a Cushman and Wakefield report.Put simply: Telecom + cloud + AI + regulation is turning the network into a strategic asset—one that must be engineered for trust, sovereignty, and intelligence.India’s telecom industry is entering a new phaseIndia’s telecom story in 2026 is not just about “more subscribers”. It is about new network architectures and new monetisation opportunities. 5G at scale is now a national layer, not a metro experiment. DoTs’ year-end review highlights near-universal district availability and the 5G BTS footprint. Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) is emerging as a key broadband lever. TRAI reports 5G FWA growth (with Jio and Airtel as the two providers reporting 5G FWA subscribers), making FWA a practical instrument for last-mile broadband expansion beyond fibre constraints. India’s  5G Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) subscriber base crossed the 10-million mark in November 2025, rising to 10.41 million according to TRAI’s telecom subscription data as of November 30, 2025, released on December 31, 2025.IoT/ Machine-to-machine (M2M) is rising—TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India)  reported M2M cellular mobile connections increasing to ~98.87 million by end-Oct 2025, a strong signal that IoT is moving into mainstream deployment. TRAI has recently released recommendations on establishing a regulatory framework for the sale of foreign telecom service providers’ SIM and eSIM cards used in M2M and Internet of Things (IoT) devices that are meant exclusively for export. The move is aimed at unlocking India’s export potential in connected devices and at the same time ensuring regulatory clarity, national security, and ease of doing business which are absolutely essential in order to sustain growth.This matters because very clearly  the telecom business model is shifting from B2C price-and-coverage to B2B2X platforms—where telecom capabilities are packaged into higher-value services (edge compute, managed connectivity services, security signals, network APIs, private networks and industry specific solutions).DPDP operationalisation changes the “rules of trust” for telecom — And for everyone who runs on telecomWith the Government of India notifying the DPDP Rules, 2025, the DPDP Act is now fully operationalised. This is not a narrow legal event. It changes telecom’s strategic role in three ways:Telcos become the “trust substrate” for the digital economyTelecom operators sit on identity-adjacent data, device signals, location and network metadata, and customer interaction layers. Under DPDP, the bar rises on how personal data is collected, processed, protected, and governed.For telcos, “privacy by design” now  becomes a product feature, not just compliance. For enterprises, a telco’s compliance posture increasingly becomes part of vendor due diligence.Data governance moves from policy decks to operational engineeringDPDP pushes organisations toward structured governance—consent, purpose limitation, security safeguards, breach readiness, grievance mechanisms, and accountability.For telecom, this will accelerate investments in:Modernised consent and preference management,Stronger encryption/tokenisation,Audit-ready observability and access controls, andShared controls across partners in the value chain (cloud, CPaaS, vendors).It amplifies the demand for “sovereign-ready” cloud and AI deploymentsDPDP doesn’t automatically mandate blanket localisation for everything—but in practice, enterprises and government workloads will increasingly demand data residency, controllable access, and auditability. This becomes a key tailwind for India-hosted cloud regions, sovereign cloud offerings, and telco-led edge/cloud propositions.Sovereignty is now a technology architecture, not a political sloganIn 2026, “sovereignty” in digital infrastructure is best understood as control:Control over where data is stored/processed,Control over who can access it (and under what legal jurisdiction),Control over security posture and audit evidence, andControl over business continuity during geopolitical or supply-chain disruptions.India is actively building ecosystem capacity for AI compute and broader AI infrastructure. The Government of India initiated the IndiaAI Mission in March 2024, with a ₹10,371.92 crore outlay) to strengthen AI capabilities, including compute access ( 38,000 GPUs deployed)  and ecosystem building.  Guided by the mission of “ AI in India and making AI work for India”,  the objective is to make  India a global leader in Artificial Intelligence in the years to come.For telecom leaders, the strategic question becomes:Can we offer “sovereign-grade connectivity + sovereign-grade cloud/edge + sovereign-grade security con

articles.heading: Telecom 2026 — Global trends powering India's connectivity revolution | Communications Today
articles.content: Telecom has evolved from a voice-centric utility into the vital artery of India’s digital ambitions. It now underpins everything – from UPI transactions to precision farming – connecting urban landscapes to remote villages and fueling the world’s fastest-growing digital economy. As 2026 unfolds, Indian telcos stand poised for a transformative leap, blending domestic resilience with global innovations in AI, satellites and next-gen networks. This piece charts the industry’s outlook and emerging trends, highlighting pathways to sustained leadership.Robust financial foundations amid rising demandIndia’s telecom sector will demonstrate resilience through macroeconomic tailwinds in 2026. According to ICRA, industry revenues will grow 10-12 percent year-on-year, fueled by tariff hikes and ARPU increases. Crisil forecasts double-digit operating profit growth, anchored by expanding 5G adoption and rising data consumption, particularly in rural areas where internet penetration accelerates. Yet this growth demands vigilance against fraud losses, estimated in hundreds of millions globally according to Juniper Research.Strengthening networks for sustainable progress5G rollouts will continue thoughtfully through 2026, pushing deeper into high-traffic urban clusters and semi-urban hotspots where upgrades make a tangible difference. Operators will emphasize refarming spectrum efficiently, optimizing existing infrastructure and maximizing performance across busy corridors. Data usage will climb steadily, driven by video streaming, entertainment apps and other services. This will trigger steady capacity boosts, smarter network modernization and energy-efficient deployments to handle the surge without compromising stability.Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) will gain ground as a practical alternative to wired broadband, especially in hard-to-reach last-mile areas. It will offer quick onboarding for households and small businesses where traditional fiber proves costly or complex. Adoption will target specific demand pockets, balancing inclusion with sustainable monetization. Quality of Service (QoS) will also take center stage. Operators and partners will align around reliable speeds, lower latency and predictable performance across all usage scenarios. This customer-first mindset will link investments directly to on-the-ground results, building trust and keeping everyone competitive.Financial discipline will remain key, striking a balance between network upgrades and long-term viability. Cybersecurity will get a major push with layered defenses for critical infrastructure and sensitive data flows. Trust will become the foundation for broader digital inclusion. Innovation will flourish through practical collaborations between operators, tech partners, startups and academia. These partnerships will test solutions in live environments, ensuring they work seamlessly and deliver real value rather than staying theoretical.Key trends reshaping connectivityGlobal forecasts spotlight trends converging on India in 2026, blending opportunity with urgency. These cluster into four pivotal shifts.AI agents revolutionizing customer experience.In 2026, AI will evolve from chatbots to modular problem-solvers which will automate most customer interactions, slashing costs while boosting satisfaction. Indian telcos can deploy AI for proactive tariff plans and network issue resolution, aligning with GenAI-fueled data spikes. Integrating these into national digital public infrastructure promises seamless expansion for initiatives like BharatNet.Satellite and NTN – Bridging the coverage divide.Multi-orbit networks blending LEO, MEO and GEO will optimize latency and resilience in 2026. Hybrid 5G-NTN models will extend connectivity to remote users.eSIM simplification.Travel eSIMs will promise predictable revenues with streamlined eSIM trends positioning operators as regional hubs.Fraud combatA defining priority in 2025 was the concerted push to curb spam calls, scam messages and digital frauds that undermine consumer trust. Telecom operators have implemented a comprehensive suite of measures under TRAI’s TCCCPR framework, including PE–TM binding, DLT-based header and content registration, and analytics-driven spam identification across voice and SMS. Building on this, all operators successfully implemented the P/S/T/G suffix framework for commercial SMS headers during the year, enabling consumers to immediately distinguish between promotional, service, transactional and Government communications.These interventions have led to a tangible reduction in spam on traditional telecom channels. However, a growing proportion of unsolicited and fraudulent communications has migrated to app-based communication platforms, which currently remain outside the telecom regulatory framework. This regulatory asymmetry weakens consumer protection and places additional financial and operational strain on telecom networks.Against this backdrop, a significant milestone was the Department of Telecommunications’ landmark decision to mandate SIM binding for app-based communication services—a first-of-its-kind global regulatory measure. Continuous SIM binding ensures that communication applications remain persistently linked to the verified mobile number used at registration, substantially strengthening accountability and traceability in cases of misuse or fraud. Telecom operators have strongly endorsed this measure, recognising it as a critical pillar in India’s efforts to combat cyber fraud and restore trust in digital communications.Spectrum and infrastructure challengesSpectrum policy remained a defining issue in 2025, with the 6 GHz band at the centre of industry and policy focus.
